issues.legal_issue: A court may permit withdrawal of a criminal prosecution only when, after considering the relevant circumstances, withdrawal would advance the interests of justice; prolonged proceedings and the accused’s non-habitual status alone do not justify withdrawal when the prosecution is nearly complete.
material_facts: The prosecution arose from allegations of assault, threats and damage to property.
Five prosecution witnesses had been examined, and the case was listed for examination of the accused when the prosecutor sought withdrawal.
The prosecutor’s application relied on the accused not being a habitual criminal.
The High Court permitted withdrawal on the basis that the accused had suffered mental harassment during a trial lasting over seven years, without examining why the case had taken so long.
The complainant had cooperated, the police had taken about three years to submit their final report, and the case had been adjourned repeatedly.
The Magistrate and the Sessions Court had rejected the withdrawal application and the resulting challenge.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s order permitting withdrawal was set aside, and the case was restored for continuation and decision on the merits because the stated reasons did not establish that withdrawal would serve the interests of justice.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 321 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the prosecutor must independently and in good faith consider the material, and the court must exercise judicial discretion to ensure that withdrawal advances the broader cause of public justice and does not stifle the prosecution. Consent is appropriate only on valid reasons, assessed in light of all relevant circumstances; it may be justified, for example, where the case is likely to end in acquittal and continuation would severely harass the accused, or where withdrawal would resolve the dispute in the interests of justice. The court’s role is supervisory rather than adjudicatory, and it need not give a detailed reasoned order when granting consent if the record shows an overall consideration of the material. These principles are drawn from State of Bihar v. Ram Naresh Pandey, State of Orissa v. Chandrika Mohapatra, Balwant Singh v. State of Bihar, Sheonandan Paswan v. State of Bihar, and Abdul Karim v. State of Karnataka.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_permission_to_withdraw and prosecutor_sought_withdrawal and accused_was_not_habitual and trial_was_prolonged and prosecution_was_nearly_complete and permission_resting_on_delay_and_non_habitual_status and no_case_specific_basis_showed_withdrawal_served_justice

predicates.appeal_challenges_permission_to_withdraw: An appeal challenges a court order permitting withdrawal of a criminal prosecution.
predicates.prosecutor_sought_withdrawal: The prosecutor applied to withdraw the prosecution.
predicates.accused_was_not_habitual: The prosecutor relied on the accused not being a habitual criminal.
predicates.trial_was_prolonged: The proceedings had lasted for a prolonged period, in part because of delays in filing the final report and repeated adjournments.
predicates.prosecution_was_nearly_complete: The prosecution had examined five witnesses and the case was about to proceed to examination of the accused.
predicates.permission_resting_on_delay_and_non_habi: The court permitted withdrawal on the basis of the prolonged trial and the accused’s non-habitual status.
predicates.no_case_specific_basis_showed_withdrawal: The court did not verify the reasons for the delay or identify a case-specific basis for finding that withdrawal would advance the interests of justice.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges permission to withdraw a prosecution, and the prosecutor relies on non-habitual status while a prolonged trial is nearly complete, permission resting on those circumstances without a case-specific basis for serving justice must be set aside and the prosecution restored.
